title: JSON Web Key (JWK)
summary: A JSON Web Key (JWK) is a JSON data structure that represents a cryptographic key. The specification also defines a JWK Set, a structure that represents a set of JWKs. Algorithms and identifiers are described in the JSON Web Algorithms specification.

plainLanguage.summary: A JSON Web Key (JWK) represents a cryptographic key as a JSON object. A JWK Set groups several keys in one JSON object, giving software a common way to exchange key information.

subtitle: A JSON format for describing cryptographic keys and sets of keys used by JOSE protocols.

tldr.problem: Software using JSON Web Signature and JSON Web Encryption needs a shared representation for cryptographic keys.
tldr.mechanism: A JWK is a JSON object containing a required key type and key-specific values, with optional use, operation, algorithm, identifier, and certificate parameters. A JWK Set contains an array of JWKs.
tldr.outcome: The format supports keys used with JWS and JWE. Private or symmetric key material must be protected from disclosure, and can be carried in an encrypted JWE.

sections.title: What a JWK Represents
sections.content:
A JSON Web Key (JWK) is a JSON data structure that represents a cryptographic key. Its members describe properties of the key, including its value. A JWK Set is a JSON object whose required keys member contains an array of JWKs.

JWKs and JWK Sets are used by JSON Web Signature (JWS, RFC 7515) and JSON Web Encryption (JWE, RFC 7516). Algorithms and identifiers are specified separately in JSON Web Algorithms (JWA, RFC 7518). The specification aims for compact representations and does not aim to replace X.509 certificates.
sections.plainLanguage: A JWK is a JSON object that describes one cryptographic key. A JWK Set is a JSON object that groups an array of those key descriptions.

sections.title: An Example Elliptic-Curve Key
sections.content:
The RFC's example JWK represents an Elliptic Curve key on the P-256 curve. It includes the key type EC, the curve name P-256, base64url-encoded x and y coordinates, and a key identifier in kid.

Appendix A provides further examples of public, private, and symmetric keys, including EC and RSA keys. RSA integers in the examples use base64url-encoded big-endian representations.
sections.plainLanguage: The example stores the curve name, encoded public-key coordinates, and a key identifier as named JSON members. Other examples show how JWKs represent different key types.

sections.title: JWK Members and Key Sets
sections.content:
A JWK is a JSON object with common parameters and parameters specific to its key type. Member names MUST be unique. A parser MUST reject a JWK with duplicate names or use a JSON parser that returns only the lexically last duplicate. Implementations MUST ignore additional members they do not understand.

Every JWK MUST include kty, the case-sensitive key-type parameter, such as RSA or EC. A JWK Set MUST include a keys array. Implementations SHOULD ignore entries with an unknown key type, missing required members, or values outside supported ranges. Array order does not indicate preference unless an application defines such a meaning.
sections.plainLanguage: Every JWK must name its key type, and each member name may appear only once. A JWK Set stores keys in an array, whose order has no default preference meaning.

sections.title: Use, Operations, Algorithms, and Key IDs
sections.content:
The optional use member says whether a public key is for signatures (sig) or encryption (enc). The optional key_ops array lists permitted operations, such as sign, verify, encrypt, or decrypt. Operation values MUST NOT be duplicated, and unrelated operations SHOULD NOT be combined for one key.

The optional alg member identifies the intended algorithm. The optional kid member helps select a key, for example from a JWK Set during key rollover. Keys in one set SHOULD normally have distinct key IDs. The use and key_ops members SHOULD NOT both be present; if both are present, their meanings MUST be consistent.
sections.plainLanguage: Optional members can describe what a key is for, which operations it permits, which algorithm uses it, and how an application identifies it. If purpose and operation members are both present, they must agree.

sections.title: Linking a JWK to an X.509 Certificate
sections.content:
Four optional parameters associate a JWK with an X.509 certificate or certificate chain. x5u gives a URI for a PEM-encoded certificate or chain; retrieving it requires integrity protection, and HTTP retrieval MUST use TLS with the server identity validated. x5c carries an array of base64-encoded DER certificates, with the certificate containing the key first.

x5t and x5t#S256 carry base64url-encoded SHA-1 and SHA-256 certificate thumbprints. For each parameter, the public key in the first certificate MUST match the public key described by the other JWK members. Any accompanying use or algorithm members MUST agree with the certificate.
sections.plainLanguage: A JWK may include a certificate, a link to one, or a certificate thumbprint. The public key in the certificate must match the key described in the JWK.

sections.title: Encrypting Private or Symmetric Keys
sections.content:
Private and symmetric key information MUST be protected from parties without legitimate access. The RFC recommends an Encrypted JWK: a JWE whose plaintext is the UTF-8 encoding of a JWK. An Encrypted JWK Set uses a JWE whose plaintext is the UTF-8 encoding of a JWK Set.

The JWE cty header parameter MUST be jwk+json for a JWK or jwk-set+json for a set, unless the application already knows the content type by another means. Encrypted JWKs are processed like other JWEs.
sections.plainLanguage: Do not expose private or symmetric key values to unauthorized parties. The RFC recommends encrypting a JWK or JWK Set as a JWE when it contains non-public key material.

sections.title: Key Trust and Protection
sections.content:
Applications must address the security issues that apply to cryptographic systems, including protecting private and symmetric keys. A key's trustworthiness depends on how it was obtained and on the trustworthiness of the entity that associates information with it. Applications may bind attributes to a JWK through mechanisms such as a PKIX certificate or a JWT.

RSA key blinding, a defense against some timing attacks, requires the RSA values n, e, and d. The RFC advises avoiding private-key representations that omit e when RSA key blinding is needed. Key entropy and random-value considerations are covered by the JWS specification.
sections.plainLanguage: A JWK's presence does not prove that its key is trustworthy. Applications must establish where the key came from and protect private or symmetric key information.

items.title: kty
items.text: Required key type, such as RSA or EC.

items.title: use
items.text: Optional intended public-key use, such as sig or enc.

items.title: key_ops
items.text: Optional list of permitted key operations.

items.title: kid
items.text: Optional key identifier used to select a key.
